chunks: Ali ibn Muhammad and Muhammad ibn al-Hasan, from Sahl ibn Ziyad, from Muhammad ibn al-Walid whose nickname is Shabab al-Sayrafi, from Dawud ibn al-Qasim al-Ja'fari who said:
I said to Abu Ja'far the Second (peace be upon him): May I be sacrificed for you, what is Al-Samad? He said: The Master to whom one turns in matters great and small.

key_terms.السَّيِّد: Al-Sayyid — the Master, Lord, or Chief; here applied to God as the supreme sovereign
key_terms.الصَّمَد: Al-Samad — a Divine Name from Surah al-Ikhlas (112:2), classically understood as 'the Eternal Refuge,' 'the Self-Sufficient,' or 'He who is depended upon'
key_terms.الْمَصْمُود: Al-Masmud — the passive participle of samada, meaning 'the one who is resorted to/turned to'; explains the root meaning of samad as intentional turning toward a master in need
key_terms.جُعِلْتُ فِدَاكَ: Ju'iltu fidak — 'May I be made your ransom/sacrifice,' a deferential formula of address used with the Imams

ai.seo_question: What does Al-Samad mean according to Imam al-Jawad?
ai.summary: This hadith records Dawud ibn al-Qasim al-Ja'fari asking Imam Muhammad al-Jawad (AS) — the ninth Imam — about the meaning of the Divine Name 'Al-Samad' from Surah al-Ikhlas (112:2). The Imam defines it as 'the Master to whom one turns in all matters, whether small or great,' emphasizing that God is the ultimate recourse for every need. This practical definition situates Al-Samad not merely as an abstract theological attribute but as a description of God's functional role as the one to whom all creation constantly turns in dependence.
word_analysis: your ransom/sacrifice (may I be sacrificed for you)
